did_you_know.text: The prophecy opens with an explicit command to Jeremiah to write all the words of the Lord in a book, so that the message about the future would be preserved and passed down through the generations.
The promise includes both Israel and Judah: the Lord will restore them to the land He gave their ancestors, and they will possess it again.
The distress is described using the image of childbirth: the men clutch their waists in pain, and every face turns pale with fear.
Although the day described is called a time of trouble for Jacob, the verse emphasizes that Jacob will be saved out of the trouble.
The symbol of slavery is a yoke placed on the neck and bonds that restrain a person; the Lord promises to break the yoke and tear off the bonds.
After being freed from slavery, Israel will serve the Lord and “David their king,” whom the Lord will raise up for them.
The Lord promises not to destroy Israel: He will discipline them justly, but He will not wipe them out, while the nations among whom they were scattered are destined for destruction.
Israel’s condition is described as a mortal wound and an incurable injury, the result of numerous sins and offenses.
Alongside the description of destruction comes a promise of healing and restoration: the Lord will heal Zion’s wounds and restore her status.
The people’s future leadership is not described as a foreign power: “One of their own” will become their ruler, and he will be able to approach the Lord.
